en: First Canto: Now, upon the plateau of Mālyavat, the arrival of the rainy season came to the descendant of Kakutstha, who was separated from his beloved,
bringing with it an irresistible surge of tears.
The rain of the clouds ceased upon the lap of that mountain,
yet the continuous stream of Rāma’s tears did not cease.
The cooing of peacocks here and there underwent a transformation;
it became the lamentation of Rāma: "O beloved princess! 1.3.
A certain indescribable splendor belonged to the stainless Sūrya and Candramas;
likewise, the radiance of the two sons of Daśaratha was such that it could not be surpassed by any union.
The cloudless sky shone with its spotless moon, and the lake gleamed with full-blown lotuses;
yet both brothers grew faint, their faces bathed in tears.
A thicket of *kuṭaja* trees arose like a web of longing for what was to be remembered;
likewise, Rāma’s mind became agitated with yearning.
The sprouting once again was undertaken by the pure *kacchaketaka* trees;
the son of the Sun did not begin anything comparable to such an act of assistance.
The wind, bearing the fragrance of plucked mālatī flowers and bringing news of Maithilī, attended upon Rāghava; yet Hanumān did not attend upon him while he was thus distressed.
With their courses now clearly visible due to the departure of the floods, the rivers shone forth as if declaring: "Sītā does not dwell among us."
When Rāma, pained by the fresh separation, was brought to the brink of death,
surely it was because of that remorse that the rows of clouds arrived.
The sky, its veil of clouds released, repeatedly seemed to entreat Rāghava for reflection with its upward-looking cranes' cries, as if filled with discursive thought.
As he searched for that thief, the quarters of the sky appeared to flee far away in fear, as if guilty of obstructing his path. (Rc 1.12)

As if because of the particularity of that specific physical appearance, the marshy thickets bore the onset of graying hair under the guise of *kāśa* grass, as though to say, "Such is the hardship [of this state]."
As it were, beholding that piteous condition of the Lord of Maithilī,
the heart of the Earth split asunder under the guise of a mass of dried mud.
Through their attenuation and incompleteness resulting from the cessation of rain,
the clouds attained a state of common studenthood with him.
The conflagration of separation that befell the lotus-pond and the royal swan passed away;
but for Sītā and Rāmabhadra, who were like two oceans of boundless sorrow, it did not.
The mountain peaks, with their streams resounding with the gurgling of tranquil waterfalls, appeared as if they were listening intently to Rāma’s clear discourse.
Even though their flowering season had passed, the rows of Kadamba forests caused him wonder with the blossoming buds that resembled smiles.
Before him, rows of dancing wagtails were seen;
and sighing, he remembered the playful movements of his beloved’s eyes.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, who knew the proper time, having bowed to Rāma— who was unable to endure separation from Rāmā— spoke for the sake of acting at that very moment.
Behold, it has become dawn, stainless; the night of the rainy season has passed.
This is the moment for the blossoming of the lotus of your enthusiasm.
The trees on the banks gain height; the soma-pressers [gain] vigor;
the lords of cattle take up intoxication; and those desiring victory take up their exertion.
"Be gracious; let Karna be given away! These riverbanks, impassable with mud, seem to entreat him to move elsewhere by means of the crying ospreys. (Rāmāyaṇa 1.23)
On this earth, it is now the time for the sun’s rays and your arrows to fall upon the enemies;
that ill-fated time has passed away.
The rivers, though their far-reaching banks were high and their depths not shallow, were crossed as if by bridges by means of trees fallen during the flood.
Like great rivers and noble women, they shine even in times of adversity through both their revealed purity and their two banks— just as rivers shine by their two shores.
In this [lake], a complete abundance of water-born flowers, birds that frequent the water, and the very support of the water itself is observed at every spot. (Rc 1.27)
With their banks eroded by the streams uprooted in their impetuous desire to fight,
the rutting bulls, lowing with passion, cause the worlds to sink downward.
O Lord of the Universe, place your trust; these clouds do not return.
These parrots, intent upon the rice stalks, are turning the quarters of the sky dark green. (Rc 1.29)
Now these deer are flocking to this ripened field of rice,
looking up at you as if you were the seeker of their desires presiding over Sāketa.
"Let some task or other be undertaken; why, noble sir, do you remain idle?
Will this [task] come to us of its own accord, even though it is desired by us? (Rc 1.31)
"Seated for victory, with the weight of your body entrusted to me, let this stone—disordered by your fainting and rolling—be cast aside. (Rc 1.32)
Let the water droplets from the tips of the leaves in the groves on the foothills be shaken off for a moment, so that your matted locks, which now conceal your shoulders, may be cleared.
"O Noble One, let your hand be withdrawn from my cheek for a moment;
let this bark-garment fastened around my shoulder be loosened, for it has grown weary."
Let arrows, their mechanisms moistened with oil, be drawn out from here and discharged;
let him take up his long bow, from which the worn-out, damp cloth has been removed.
"Descend from this chariot; let this ill-health be cast off.
Slay the Ten-necked one with arrows purified by piercing the ten directions."
Take the straight path; the patched garment of worldly action is heavy. Drive this darkness of "what-should-be-done-ness" far away. (Rc 1.37)
For the Noble One, there is only auspiciousness; your enemy has already been slain.
Enough with giving away your body—the refuge of the three worlds—only to bring about its own destruction.
"Who is this wretched Rākṣasa that, while your bow is strung, has been driven far away by this despondency of yours? (Rc 1.39)
With your entire bodily sustenance wiped away by the force of tears, fainting spells, and lamentations, that month of Prauṣṭhapada has passed for you.
Now let enthusiasm be exerted; let the destruction of the enemy be considered.
For those great beings who have their own arms as allies, what restraint can there be upon themselves?

May there be well-being for you now, O best of men, a true elephant among men, whose speed is unimpeded, and who possesses a hide-rope like a cloud torn asunder by the wind of the month of Bhādrapada.
Be gracious and undertake the journey of bodily existence once more, however it may be;
for Lakṣmaṇa does not disregard the command of those who are younger than you.
The unfathomable fortitude of this noble one is sung of throughout the three worlds; what is this lifelong undertaking, which is fit only for an ordinary person?
O noble one, who can withstand the torrent of arrows from you when you are enraged— arrows that extinguish the fierce fire-like luster of Jamadagnya?
While you thus despair, having cast off the burden of your own duty,
the enemy with the fangs of Death will not yet have become your guest.
It is known that he is an assassin, yet it has been heard that he lives as an honorable man;
since the time for action has arrived, what is the point of wasting time?
The supreme and manifest abode of that deceitful enemy is not known;
however, his friend Sugrīva has promised to search for him.
The lord of monkeys, whose renowned troop of monkeys has been summoned from every quarter, will surely fall at the feet of my noble brother this very moment. (Rāmāyaṇa 1.49)
The sky will become tawny from the impact of the swift throngs of monkeys, as if vying with the surface of the earth that is golden-hued with ripening rice.
Soon, with their faces radiant with fury,
the sky will appear as if covered by a hundred rising suns.
Oh, what brilliance! Oh, what loveliness! Oh, what character! Oh, what strength!
Oh, what power! Oh, what devotion! Oh, what wisdom belongs to Hanumān!
Surely, for our sake, that bold and vigilant inner minister does not allow Sugrīva to sleep.
And surely even his minister Jāmbavān, advanced in wisdom and age, is respectfully urging him on to repay that favor.
Thus, for what reason does the lord of men delay?
For such a person would not be one who maintains virtuous servants if he were ungrateful.
He who has sought out the noble path must certainly return;
for the exertion of those who have undertaken another's task is indeed exceedingly intense. (Rc 1.56)
Or rather, with his eyes closed in the bliss of enjoyment obtained through your grace,
he did not perceive those quarters of the sky that were shrouded in mist.
But for how long will that cry of the swans in the pleasure-ponds, intoxicated with passion, no longer reach his ears? (Rc 1.58)
What is the use of further words? Today or tomorrow will come the Lord of the Monkeys, who is true to his promise and who has made Kiṣkindhā anxious with longing.
Even if there is a difference [between us], O Noble One, let that which is to be done be considered;
let the accomplishment of our task be accepted by you, for it is not to be set aside by delay.
He who was previously assisted by the Noble One, even though he now acts ignobly, might remain cool; or rather, who can truly know the minds of others? (Rc 1.61)
"He, though prosperous, has as if forgotten the promise he made to us;
go quickly, noble sir, and remind him—what patience can one have when tormented by a task? (Rc 1.62)
I shall awaken him with words that contain the inner essence of the staff;
for conciliation merely lulls those who are heedless and attached to pleasure.
Be gracious; let delusion be conquered, and let it be discerned: "Who am I?
The ocean of calamity has already been crossed; how insignificant is this [delusion]! (Rc 1.64)
Delighted by these truthful words of Saumitri, which rained down nectar,
the scion of Raghu seemed to conquer the internal surge of his anguish.
He opened his eyes and looked slightly toward the quarters;
then he raised himself from the edge of the couch, loosening his long, eyelash-fringed matted locks.
In a certain nearby, pure place where the dust had been swept away by the long hair of Saumitri as he hurriedly bowed down, he sat upon a stone slab.
Seated there without Sītā, Rāma did not shine,
like the raised banner of Indra when it is devoid of its victory-flag.
To his younger brother, who was seated nearby like Indra before the enemy of the Danavas,
he spoke words faltering with affection.
"Come, come! Delight me with an embrace and your dear conversation;
for my tears flow incessantly, and I cannot even look at you, Lakṣmaṇa."
Alas, my child! This same condition has now come upon your limbs as well.
Let that wretched Rāma be restrained, for he is tormenting our sole kinsman.
"My child, there is no remedy for this disease born of misfortune, by the protraction of which this nectar of your consolation has been exhausted. (Rc 1.72)
"O child, though shaken by the repeated assault of many irresistible and terrible afflictions, my life-breaths do not depart because of your consolation."
"O child, remembering the cutting of my father Jaṭāyu’s vital organs— my dear friend who had his wings clipped by my enemy— I cannot bear it."
I alone, a sinner, have become the cause for the death of those two, my father’s father and his friend, who were both so affectionate toward their children. (Rc 1.75)
The grief born from the abduction of one's beloved would be stilled once the enemy was properly uprooted;
however, this anger of mine, which arises from the calamity of my father and friend, has death itself as its limit.
As the lord of birds fell from the surface of the sky with his wings severed, my friend spoke to him, saying, "Who else is there? Do not fear! (Rc 1.77)
"O child, what other man besides the wretched Rāma could be so impotent, he who does not protect his devoted wife who has followed him from her enemy? (Rc 1.78)
By her, while we two were suffering in the hardships of the Daṇḍaka forest, even as ascetics, our faces were not turned away from them.
The daughter of the King of Videha and daughter-in-law of Daśaratha wandered from forest to forest, thinking, "My son-in-law has been killed."
"By me, who neither nourished my own body nor protected my wife, has some eunuch equal to me been born in the lineage of Raghu. (Raghuvamśa 1.81)
O Lakṣmaṇa, it is not only you who are my good brother as you lament thus repeatedly; even the animals in this forest have been made to weep by me.
While the clouds were arrayed in all directions as witnesses to my terrible affliction,
the mountain streams, resembling cascading waterfalls, carried away the tears of the trees.
Even by the sounds of the tender, fresh rain-clouds heard from afar,
the peacocks did not dance in the forest out of compassion for me.
"Sugrīva will surely come; Janakī truly lives.
Your word does not fail—brother, speak it again and again! (Rāmāyaṇa 1.85)
With the outward flow of my breath obstructed by these spray-like drops of your words,
the embers of Sītā’s separation lick at my vital organs within.
For this reason as well, this other fire burns me intensely:
that an arrow was released at Vālin, who dwelt in the forest free from enmity.
Moreover, I would feel a heavy shame now, like a debtor being pursued by creditors,
since we, O monkeys, must seek a return for the favor received.
There is no hope for a return favor from that fickle monkey,
by whom this exceedingly light-handed one has leaped upon the lofty tree of truth.
"Arise, child; let us go and now accomplish our purpose elsewhere.
Sugrīva, preoccupied with the pleasures of his new sovereignty, will not come. (Rc 1.90)
Let the ascetic rejoice thus, having been reunited with his wife after a long time;
yet, being tormented by her affection, how can he remain free from distress?
Moreover, my child, we were formerly friends because our circumstances were equal;
but now that he is blinded by vast wealth, who are we to him?
Even one who has grasped the path of the virtuous, having suddenly attained prosperity, falls—utterly negligent and stumbling—upon a path beset with pitfalls. (Rc 1.93)
Rare indeed is that person, O child, whose mind is not instantly robbed by the intoxication of prosperity, which resounds like an echo at the time of calamity.
Whether he be virtuous or unvirtuous, he need not be scrutinized by me now;
my heart, my child, does not venture to bestow its favor upon him.
"This one who has not yet arrived is superior; let him be turned away as he approaches, my child.
Wise men do not admit a friend when they are in a crisis involving their own interests. (Rc 1.96)
"Wherever a virtuous person finds one fallen into misfortune, they must offer assistance;
yet we have made that wretched wager without due reflection. (Rc 1.97)
Was it like a skeleton from the edge of Mount Mandara, with hundreds of jackals sleeping within,
that was cast down by me, as if by the man who gave instructions to Dundubhi?
For what purpose were the seven *sāla* trees pierced by you, O ascetic? Let that fool believe it was for me; why not have accomplished this elsewhere?
What youth of the warrior class, lacking the true nature of a kṣatriya, would discharge an arrow like Rāma against Vālī while he was preoccupied, for the sake of the beast Sugrīva?
The path that can be described as the mire of worldly existence is not abandoned so long as one does not surrender oneself to the task of closing off the difficult [passage].
"O Valīmukha, you were pierced by me with but a single arrow while I was still a fool;
yet he has planted in me those word-arrows which are impossible to extract."

"O child, how many times more shall I remember [my past], having not yet reached the further shore of calamity? Instruct me in what is appropriate for the occasion; Rāma does not perceive anything at all."
Support me, O brother, for I am unable to endure the memory of Sītā;
my mind, though striving to go far away, is being robbed by delusion.
"O child, for me who dwell in the forests with both sides protected by you and her, no hardship whatsoever has arisen. (Rāmāyaṇa 1.105)
"Alas, timid one! Alas, dearest one! Alas, you who are distressed by separation from me!
Where are you?"—uttering these half-spoken words, he fell unconscious to the ground.
"O mother Kaikeyī, you are satisfied; enjoy the kingdom free from thorns!"—saying this, Lakṣmaṇa fell at his lotus-feet.
Then, with tearful eyes and watched by the distressed deer, the two of them fell down like the sun and moon fallen from the sky, watched by the distressed [beings].
When those two, the sons of Daśaratha, had thus fallen upon the surface of the earth,
the radiance [of the sun] was abandoned by all ten faces of the lady of the quarters, as if out of a lack of fortitude.
Triumphant are these feet of the illustrious crown prince Hāravarṣa— the moon upon the earth for one who relishes his desires to their full—
by which was produced the great blossoming of the night-lily that is Abhinanda, a bloom otherwise difficult to overcome by the mass of rays from twelve suns.
Thus ends the first canto in the great poem *Rāmacarita* composed by Abhinanda. **The Second Canto:** Then Lakṣmaṇa, having restrained that unprecedented agitation of his own, [spoke].
With intense anger, he spoke these words to his deluded elder brother for the sake of consolation: "Rc_2.1"
"Noble sir, let the remaining task be told; let this darkness born of improper application be dispelled.
May your lotus-face soon blossom at the rising of the sun that is royal exertion. (Rc 2.2)
This is the time for us to remain together; do not resort to such delusion.
Indeed, exert yourself, for that which was long desired is now within reach of those who rejoice.
We are merely consumers of the fruit; we have no certainty that he is in the abode of that thief.
Let the Son of the Sun approach, and even this darkness shall vanish in an instant.
Rulers, for reasons of state, slay even their own biological sons as if they were enemies;
why do you, like an ordinary man, feel remorse because of the punishment of the monkey who was a foe to his younger brother?
What harm is there for archers sporting in the deer-parks even when they slaughter ten million living beings?
Why do you grieve incessantly; why was the killing of a single monkey committed without purpose?
And why is that aged Jaṭāyu now mourned, who, having cast off his worn-out body, has purchased for himself a fame as radiant as the rays of the moon? (Rc 2.7)
Let this single day pass; tomorrow that king of monkeys will not be awaited.
Therefore, be gracious and search all around yourself for the earth, with its mountains and oceans.
Just as the meeting of Kabandha, Śabarī, and Hanumān occurred for us, will not some other auspicious encounter likewise befall us again, like that of the forest and the mountain traveler? 2.9.
Wherever you achieve success, who could possibly thwart your desire?
Not only has that evil-minded one not remained on the path of those who possess radiant knowledge; he has gone even further astray.
Either a sudden assault occurs in his city, or he incurs intense infamy—what more need be said?
For a new king, it is said, digs up a row of thorns within the very joints of his own limbs, causing him pain. (Rc 2.11)
Now, first of all, noble sir, let an effort be made to discover news of him, provided that even now he remains sincere and that the fault of delay can still be forgiven. (Rc 2.12)
"Abandon delusion; descend from here and resort to this untroubled river.
There goes the charioteer Aruṇa, ruddy as a hibiscus flower, swiftly toward the western quarter."
Hearing those words after a long time, the joy of the Raghus opened his eyes, filled with wonder;
for even those who are separated by lack of union do not fail to lie down when such favorable circumstances present themselves.

Then, beholding him whose delusion had been dispelled like the moon emerged from the clouds, Lakṣmaṇa received his speech, which was as cooling as a drop of moisture trickling from a mountain of moonstone.

Behold, this bird, its dense cage of rays shattered by the twilight that grows bold in the western quarter, has fallen from the vault of heaven and now vanishes into the thickets of the sunset mountain.

The sun, red as a *bandhujīvaka* flower, its kinship with the world distant, could be worshipped by the inhabitants of the city of Pāśapāṇi with hands not raised high, as if it were constrained by a sense of obligation.
This sun, having released his rays, performs a dance of conformity toward the Lord of Waters;
in times of adversity, it is better to abandon one's natural disposition than to act in a manner inconsistent with one's refuge.
These rays of the sun, beautiful at their base like the bimba fruit, pierce the sky;
and these long staff-like bodies of the trees fill the earth.
In front, the heat of the sun is driven away by the thickening shade of a dense cluster of peaked trees; behind, it does not quickly leave the mountain ridges, remaining closely pressed against them.
The ascetic gradually accepts the shade of trees and even the plateaus of mountain peaks;
meanwhile, his sense of ownership toward his own body in relation to the heat of the sun diminishes step by step.
The sun moves toward the western quarter, and these birds cry out in agitation;
as the day—whose end is unavoidable—fades away, darkness appears like a venomous serpent with a sight that strikes fear. (Rc 2.22)

This sacred tree at the foot of the slope, with its flocks of birds crying out, is being scattered upon by travelers at evening; it is like the home of a virtuous man, which is freely frequented by those away from home.

O gentle one, these riverbanks—where the rows of kalahamsa birds sleep at their edges, where the sand-heaps are pure with gentle waves, and where the breezes move freely through the water—become the refuge for weary travelers. (Rc 2.24)
Fie upon those white-winged birds dwelling on the riverbanks who witness the destruction of the lotus clusters!
Noble sir, I praise only that day which sets together with the friend of the lotuses.
With a single sallakī sprout tucked into the root of his tusk, followed by a languid glance,
this lordly elephant slowly proceeds toward the water, having released the mountain cave.
The elephants bathe themselves in the water scented by their own ichor,
while the breezes blowing from the edges of the ponds waft the fragrance of blooming *mālatī* groves.
The buffaloes abandon the smooth waters at the roots of the lakes and rivers;
suddenly pursued by curlews, cranes, and other buffaloes fleeing in fear, they scatter.
Behold, from the lotus grove where thick petals are joined face-to-face,
bees that have continuously drunk their fill of the gathered nectar from the calyxes are now moving toward the night-lotuses.
Neither was it a lotus with its petals closed, nor yet a night-lily with its petals released;
rather, it was a pair of leaves that had witnessed one another’s gaze, their violent agitation now subsided.
Having passed from the riverbank to the sand, and thence from that lotus-pond to the lily-lake,
the bird— his separation from his mate fresh at evening— plunges into the water as if it were fire.
Neither closing like a lotus, nor blossoming with the smile of a water-lily bud,
this pair of birds in the water remained utterly bewildered, staring intently at one another.
The sun abandons his worn-out boat of the day and no longer extends his slow-moving rays;
having reached the unseen shore, he clings solely to that which remains of the ocean of the sky.
As if hearing the sacred revelation through the warbling of birds, the world accepts the darkness with the cry of "Oṃ";
now, even the sun, deprived of its heat, is no longer able to protect its own orb.
Let it be seen: just as the sun rises, so too does it set;
Fate is the master over both joy and calamity, yet it has no power over the transformations of the great.

Behold here this flourishing cluster of lotuses, with its bed shimmering with swans and cranes, and its edges of water—still, clear, and circular—where the lotus stalks lie motionless amidst their thorns. (Rc 2.36)

These ruru deer, devoid of effort and following after their previous mouthfuls of young grass, find peaceful rest upon the cool, immovable ridges of the mountain slopes, their faces only slightly flickering.
The sun, having reached the bride of the western quarter through the twilight, abandons his familiar rays and no longer holds to even the lotuses; he has attained a certain indescribable glow.
Though the sky is devoid of sun and moon, it is stainless; though the earth is without trees or water, it is cool.
For a moment, the world shines, occupying the interval between the day and the night.
"Here is this waterfall, this river, and that clear lake and pond shine forth;
let her ladyship, the mother of our father, attend to whichever among these pleases her mind. (Rc 2.40)
Thus, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, their inner anguish concealed, completed the rites appropriate for the occasion and offered one another a mutual salutation and some indescribable request.

The two descendants of Raghu quickly reached that region which had been thoroughly examined on all sides— a place where the breeze from the night-lotus groves did not blow, and alas, where the moonlight was not to be seen.
Lakṣmaṇa cleared the ground for the bed of Rāmabhadra, sweeping it with his palm as if with a broom, removing the thorns and pits, and covering the bare earth with fresh grass.
He suddenly washed the pair of lotus-feet of the elder brother as he was about to sleep,
and out of skill, he again wiped away the water drawn up by his own garment with his lotus-like hands.
Lakṣmaṇa, shedding tears, long caressed with his hand— of which only the physical instrument remained— the foot of his elder brother, whose royal marks were worn away by the journey.
Having loosened with his fingertips the tangled forest of matted locks, he brought it into order;
and having shaken off the garment of skin that had slipped from his shoulder, he tucked its edge back into place.
He placed two great quivers at his sides and took upon his head the honored bow;
then he smoothed his rug, which had been repeatedly folded, with the hem of his own garment that was shaken and gathered up.
Thus, his forest-dwelling torments being constantly overcome by the service of those born after him,
the joy of the Raghus, with senses as languid as if wishing to sleep, lay down for a moment.

With his eyes half-closed and then opening, he slowly beheld his wakeful younger brother; placing his head upon the hollow of his elder brother’s upraised lotus-like hand, he spoke these measured words.
Go, my child, to your own bed; you are emaciated, so how much longer can you endure this suffering? Attain clarity through sleep for a moment; constant vigil throughout the night is not sustainable.
"Brother, we have much to do this morning; why are you not intent on your own affairs?
At dawn, let the meeting with that cool Lord of Monkeys be considered."
Whether he be proud of having attained his station, or whether he be one whose fortune has not yet risen, he must indeed come to us—
who are bound by our agreement— once again for the sake of a final decision.
May this night shine brightly for you as you travel happily to the palace of the king of monkeys;
and that which is appropriate for your two wings, once they have been described, shall be provided at that very moment.
Having spoken thus, the sinless younger brother became speechless, his lotus-eyes closed like buds; he silently rested near the lotus-feet of his elder brother.
And there, as the two heroes lay for a long time,
the trees— seeming as if their trepidation had vanished— proclaimed the victory over the darkness with the loud hooting of owls.
"Though you have bared your teeth and have been praised by the sun for a long time, you shall not escape now"—
thus did the darkness rise far up toward the sky, as if speaking through the cries of the enemy birds of ill omen.
Not only did the birds no longer frequent their nests, but even the trees lay dormant on all sides;
and the mountains appeared as if their splendor were being plundered by a multitude of thieves in the form of darkness.
Neither the dry land, nor the sandy banks, nor the rivers, nor the mountains, nor the trees shone;
only the all-pervasive darkness, which subverts the doctrine of duality, prevailed in its splendor.
There, in the dense darkness, the young deer, being bewildered, did not perceive even the doe standing at his side;
meanwhile, by chance, the young female ruddy goose attained union with her husband, who was trembling with longing.
Bringing the elder one onto his lap out of the delusion that he was a child, the monkey touched him limb by limb—
though his own limbs were also being touched— as rising doubt made him slowly stroke the leader of the troop, thinking, "Is this my beloved?"
The earth, though long familiar to him, could no longer be perceived— seeming as if encompassed on all sides by mountains, covered without interval by trees, and flooded here and there by waters.
In the quarters of the sky it was skillful; on the earth, unconfused; in the air, moving with great ease; in the forests, terrifying;
upon the mountains, intoxicated; in the caves, invincible; thus, darkness appeared equally pervasive across all uneven terrains.
As if sharing a common calamity, the quarters of the sky at evening united with the earth’s surface, their faces darkened;
and the heavens, its peaks seized by masses of darkness, fell down upon the ground, the friend of the earth.
Nothing clear appeared before him, nor behind him, nor at his sides;
the world was pervaded by the night’s darkness, dense as a range of peaks from the mountain of collyrium.
No second object was perceived, even when close at hand, as it was obscured by darkness;
at that time, knowledge had only the self as its object, like that of fetuses dwelling within the womb.
Even though their limbs were closely entwined, the couples suffered intensely from one another, as if afflicted by the fever born of separation,
for the nectar of beholding each other’s faces remained difficult to obtain.
Surely that wind, with its excessive spray of cold frost, scattered heaps of burning embers, since the poor young female ruddy goose cried out so piteously in distress. (Rc 2.67)
In the forest regions, that rustling sound of falling leaves did not arise;
nor did the frequent *caṭat* noise produced by the breaking of sallakī branches dragged by elephants ever resound.
The mountains stood at a distance like sentinels, their human forms embodied;
and the trees, with the tips of their tender branches bent like hands, circumambulated and served the two of them.
The forest breeze quickly dispelled the summer heat, shook off the loose dust, and blew away their tattered outer garments; thus it assumed the duty of a watchman stationed near the two of them.
As he, along with his younger brother, was fading away in the darkness, the elephants— whose intentions were as if captivated by their impending departure—
prepared for their retreat, signaled by their bright, long tusks.
Nearby, a multitude of shimmering, unshakable medicinal herbs performed the office of lamps;
and the forest deities bestowed auspicious blessings upon the two who were sleeping amidst the mountains and woods.
"Come, Jānakī, to my embrace; you are as hard as a stone, why do you turn your face away?
Rest your head upon my cheek and sleep; when will such refusal from you ever cease? (Rc 2.73)
This garment has been cast upon my breast; may you take pleasure in it, for your bosom is joyless.
O long-eyed one, show forbearance toward this hand that loosens your girdle; why do you push it away as if in anger?
The words of the Lord of Maithilī were heard by the Earth, who had approached him while tormented by separation from Maithilī and whose tears were held back by her many quarters as her companions.
"The descendant of Raghu fears separation from me, and without me the world finds no joy;
what shall I do?"—as if thinking thus, the moon did not suddenly rise.
Nothing at all appeared clearly before him;
rather, by means of a mere gesture of his hand, the darkness situated far in the sky was seen as if being threatened by someone.

A darkness, variegated by the rays of the moon-like face of the lady of the cloud-vehicled quarter (the East), enchanting with its braid filled with rows of thick *mālatī* flowers, was born. (Rc 2.78)
Embraced with affection by the foremost rays of the moon situated far away,
the sky in the direction of the enemy of Namuci rose up, its burden of dense darkness cast off.
Although the arrival of the essence of passion had been announced by the entry of rays from the brilliant tip [of the sun],
the moon was nevertheless gazed upon after a long time, facing the stage of the sky and having aroused longing.
With the remaining darkness pierced by the rising rays of the moon,
the face of the eastern quarter shone as if it were being anointed with saffron mixed with musk.
The lady of the eastern quarter did not bear that single breast, though it was red with saffron ointment, like the newly risen moon;
rather, she bore it out of longing for her lover.
Before Manmatha, whose own flower-bow had been taken up and who was about to conquer the worlds,
the ocean of milk raised up a full golden jar in the guise of the moon.
With the broad cups of the moon brought near her by the onset of the twilight,
Indra’s night shone as if intoxicated, her mass of garments— the dense darkness— now loosened and fallen away.
The moon rose, delighting the world that had long been turned upward, softening the efforts opposed by Love,
making the birds cry out for their separated mates, and thickening the joy [of those who were not].

The moon—the very life of the young woman Night—rose up like a pleasure-palace for amorous play: a single lotus in the multitude of the eyes of women, and a sandy bank for the swan of the mind to rest upon.
The moon embraced the night, made the night-lily— still possessing its buds— blossom with laughter,
seized the hands of the star-wives with his own rays, and brought the sky to a state of serene clarity.
The moon, who has the daughter of Dakṣa as his consort, assumed the vow of being markless in the sky, concealed his own spot with his rays,
and sent forth his moonlight into the quarters from which it had departed.
Then, having pervaded the far-reaching, stainless sky— which was like a lotus pond free from mud—
the foremost rays of the Lord of Night shone forth, as tender as the stalks of a pure red lotus.
In the sky, in the quarters, and upon the earth, the rays of the lord of night fell in dense masses;
here and there, the darkness of night entered certain caverns that were trembling.

In the direction of the quarters, the darkness cast by the moonbeams hung suspended from the crest of the three-eyed god’s matted hair; there it remained, driven away and rendered helpless by its pursuit, like one fleeing in all directions.
The darkness took up residence in the caves of great mountains, in the hollows of ancient trees, within the hearts of lotuses, and upon the faces of the wives of travelers.

The moon abandoned the eastern quarter, the direction of the king of gods, which had lost its redness through excessive intimacy; it took to the sky, where the girdle of stars was tossed about as it was fondled by the tips of his rays.
The moon spread its rays— showering nectar, surpassing the courtyard of the sky,
pure as the tips of *ketakī* flowers, and acting as comets for those separated from their loved ones— over the earth.
The lotuses acted rightly by shrinking away from the moon, which excels them in loveliness;
but when that victorious face of a lovely woman rose up, they committed a rash act once more.
The lord of the night, possessing a lofty orb, uprooted the anger [of the moon] and brought about the cessation of the unbearable wounds;
having removed the mud of pride, he led the loving women to the hands of their beloveds.
By means of the moonlight— which flows through manifest paths, openings, and rivers, and penetrates forests, villages, thickets, dense jungles, and mountain clefts—
the people became indifferent to the day, owing to its preeminent quality of gentleness.
The night-lotus was no longer drunk by eyes, and the moonlight scorched the red-hued coverlet;
meanwhile, the bee appeared, drinking deeply of the supreme fragrance that rose from the water, which was now devoid of support.
Though she was in the midst of her own herd, the female elephant, like one all alone, cried out in fear;
and out of apprehension, she repeatedly rubbed the base of the tusks of the male elephant with her trunk.
Upon the *ketakī* flowers, the plantains, the sands, the stones, the blooming water-lilies, and the water,
the river carrying the moon’s radiance shimmered as if it had been made to leap up in a succession of waves.
Variegated here and there by moonbeams passing through the gaps between fine, dense foliage,
the deer resting at the foot of the trees bore the graceful appearance of a herd of spotted antelopes.
Having secured their joints upon mountain peaks acquired with great difficulty, and having formed the intent to conquer the God of Love,
the moonbeams entered the lap of Rāghava, which was as difficult to approach as any woman other than the princess of Mithilā.
"Are you awake, *kāśmari*? You sit there, *kovidāra*. Where are you, dear *kṛtamāla*, *tamāla*?
Look! Thus was it said by the forest regions, who gazed upon the multitude of trees in haste, asking: "How fares the Lord of the Raghus? (Raghuvamśa 2.103)
The moonlight was indeed obstructed by trees with hundreds of broad and dense branches closely interlaced with one another;
for that moonlight was truly unwholesome for the son of Daśaratha, who was overcome by the terrible fever of separation.

Then the lily grove became sleepless for no reason, and the sky, though filled with clusters of stars, was alas, in vain; the world was born as if without a master, and even the moon at that time was pitiable, like the blooming youth of a widow.

"The daughter of Janaka sighs; the son of the Sun is in haste; the Lord of Monkeys has arrived; it is a beautiful dawn for you"—thus did certain birds, warbling sweetly in the latter part of the night, seem to sing to the Lord of the Raghus with words only half-understood.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Description of Twilight, Darkness, and the Rising of the Moon," in the great poem *Rāmacarita* composed by Abhinanda.
What is the use of other beast-like kings giving gifts to poets on such occasions? May that King Karṇa alone grant [the reward] for even a moment;
he by whom the life-story of Rāma—though its high renown in the world was not grasped even by the knowers of truth out of fear of the expenditure of vast wealth—was brought to great preeminence.
Salutation to that sovereign lord of men, the crown prince, who alone shines like a lotus grove over the lineage of the Pālas; by him,
Abhinanda— whose form was radiant with fame produced by the gift of ten million [gold pieces]— was led to the state of immortality.
The Third Canto.
Then Rāma, who had previously awakened and found pleasure in falling into a deep sleep, took hold of the feet of the son of Sumitrā as he sat there already awake, and spoke to him thus: Rc_3.1 //

Has the night been spent in this very manner? Have you perhaps slept for even half a moment? And at this opportune time for clarity, what purpose do you have established in your mind through your intellect? (Rc 3.2)

Having reflected again for the sake of ascertaining the disposition of that new lord, O forest-dwellers, quickly declare what is appropriate for the occasion; this time for departure is most auspicious.
If the monkey is rendered motionless by the attainment of his own purpose, there is no benefit in following him;
it is better to have an enemy than a friend who, though possessing wealth, is susceptible to change and doubt.
It is evident that we have been cast out today by that villain, who is devoid of hope for any other purpose;
for he has bestowed upon us from afar this "half-moon" [curse] known as a long-lasting refusal.
Why did that ascetic, blinded by pride, not stop anyone as he was falling into the dark well of delusion?
And were those inhabitants of the region—Hanumān and the others—who immediately attained his station, also destroyed along with him? (Rc 3.6)
No misfortune was seen for the son of Pavamāna, nor for the son of Agni, nor for the son of Vālin;
yet for what reason were all those monkey youths as if dead at one and the same time? (Rc 3.7)
That Hari, difficult to restrain, now lies today intoxicated by the pride of having tasted the sweetness of sovereignty;
yet it is my reflection that those who have attained him must have been asleep even during the time of his awakening.
By him— impelled by the god [Brahmā], surrounded by those powerful friends of the moon,
and possessing a magnificent bodily luster— for our sake, darkness was utterly dispelled.

Oh, what a great darkness born of delusion! For today, having violently cast aside those jewel-lamps of ministers in the midst of the assembly, this arrogant one has seized the king of the monkeys by force.
The excessive flow of greed, delusion, passion, and pride was not restrained;
yet today, by him whose desires are fully realized, the force of our desire to repay his kindness has been restrained. (Raghuvamśa 3.11)
"May we not now be for the displeasure of him who stands upon the throne of an emperor, having fallen from his position;
for even though our skill with weapons has been witnessed, have we not become a source of fear to that coward, my child? (Rc 3.12)
It was only right that that wicked soul, smooth-tongued with deceit, was cast out from his station by my wise elder brother;
yet, blinded by pride, I have once again in vain consecrated a jackal to the rank of a lion-king.
A harsh punishment destroys the sleep of deceit in lowly men who seek to evade their obligations;
nevertheless, this bow of mine must act with courtesy toward him.
As long as the sound produced by the velocity of Vālin’s bone-piercing arrow does not cease to resound in all directions,
so long might that very shaft again strike here in the three worlds at Kiṣkindhā, which has been overrun.

Out of pride, he did not announce [his deeds] to us, thinking, "He might slay the remaining enemies with his own two arms and, having established a reign of righteousness, depart. Thus, the desire for wealth sees no authority in [the king's] vision. (Rc 3.16)

Therefore, this creation of mine, though stainless in its origin, is obstructed by the sixfold group [of vices] and must be abandoned like an enemy; alas, that wing of yours which was not forbidden by me previously because I was undisciplined—[that too must now be abandoned].
Without doubt, having been informed of your proximity by the female doorkeeper in a state of agitation,
he— facing the imminent separation from his inner apartments— will harbor resentment toward you in his heart.
That face of yours, copper-red as the rising sun, will find no joy in words of affection from me;
instead, it will be shrouded in the darkness of anxiety over the burden of repaying my kindness.
Even when being reminded, he will not remember you; nor will he look upon you when questioned.
Now, dwelling in the midst of lovely women, he remains lost in thought concerning us.
As soon as he saw the city of Kālikā while we were settled on the mountain slope, that fickle man entered it; at that very moment, our friendship was violated by him.
"During these days, not even a single moment passed, nor was there a suitable messenger," and so forth—he clearly spoke such falsehoods as a pretext for reproaching you out of affection. (Rc 3.22)
Having shown contempt for you who were gracious with affection, and being unable to offer a reply when you spoke of urgent business,
the monkey will look upon your face with his mouth parched, his heart colored by a spark of anger.
"Let there be for me the non-occurrence of whatever purpose might suddenly arise from his arrival;
otherwise, the lingering anxiety over our journey to his abode—exceeding even the slaying of Vālin—will constantly afflict us both."
Surely that former circle of well-wishers was sent to the depths by him who partakes in misfortune;
now he is made to sport incessantly, day and night, by those far more clever than he.
Dice, gazelle-eyed women, hunting, honeyed drinks, and spectacles now steal his time;
the words of trusted friends and the flattering songs of wandering bards do not find a single moment of his attention.
Terrified, the ministers say nothing at all; what is the use of our anxiety?
For that king, devoted only to sensual pleasure, does not himself now connect the preceding with the following.
Neither the wise, nor the elders, nor the steadfast standing before him assume the role of judges;
rather, he remains full of doubt in the assembly while the playful women sit behind him.
This being the case, who could restrain your surging wrath when you have gone there?
Yet, upon reflection, this pursuit of slaughtering the monkeys would not lead to our welfare.
I perceive no merit in bringing back one who has approached with deceit and by force;
for such people, when standing close by, pain the ears of their enemies with their praise. (Rc 3.30)

If he has not been touched by any transformation whatsoever, nor has he now arrived here due to some necessity, let him come of his own accord; do not act in vain, for his splendor is restrained by your forceful command.
Just as it was told by our father Jaṭāyu and just as it was told by Kabandha,
so shall the golden-wheeled universal monarch, whose discus has been summoned, surely arrive before long.

Since it is true that his qualities will reach their full manifestation because they originate from the Sun, I do not suspect any discrepancy in him regarding the fault of being delayed by the impact at the tip of the scale. (Rc 3.33)
For him who had returned to his own dwelling after suffering from illness and living in a foreign land,
so many days passed solely in the agitation of being reunited with his anxious circle of kinsmen.
Surely that lord of monkeys will come; yet I do not approve of this delivery of a message.
O child, noble people do not relinquish their very essence, nor do they abandon their fortitude, even when their purpose is at stake.
With obstacles overcome and devoted to the welfare of his friends, he will not remain indifferent; what is the use of past time?
Being urged on, he will surely reach the further shore of our steadfastness with all haste.
Fie on me, who am so perverse and suspicious toward him, or rather, fie on that which is so great!
For an unfortunate person, when suspended between his own interests, first concludes only in opposition to them. (Rc 3.37)
Thus, in either of these two initial positions, there is no prospect of my survival;
it would be better to endure here for a few more days, exceeding even those counted by time.
"Now you should speak what you have reflected upon; that which is to be practiced must be done without doubt.
For from childhood onwards, your intellect has been superior and does not incline toward the prima facie position. (Rc 3.39)

Having heard these gracious words of his elder brother, the son of Sumitrā, after a long time freed from the mire of despondency, spoke this, greeting him with the very radiance of his countenance: *iti prasannāṃ giram agrajasya śrutvā cirād vītaviṣādapaṅkaḥ / mukhaśriyaivojjvalayābhinandann idaṃ sumitrātanayo jagāda //* Rc_3.40 //
The virtuous monkey has successfully accomplished everything; what need is there for further words?
Even that which was not perceived as a fault by the Noble One, though it was perfectly evident, is not considered a transgression.
The inner mind of even me does not perceive any fault in him due to his surpassing splendor;
yet I do not know why this [other] man does not recognize it, nor does he see the transgression committed by Time.
Or perhaps those Nalas and others, having been dismissed, have returned today to come back;
for he, showering down a rain of wealth from his rising treasury, gathers the most excellent horses from other regions, as the clouds gather choice stallions from distant lands.
Now, the Lord of the Monkeys, whose crest-jewel is the eighteen islands, receives back those who were formerly lost through the slaying of Vālin,
having been won over by various means and now honored with great hospitality.
To those who were not yet content, who had consumed all their possessions without sharing them, and who were without means of transport, he—
having entrusted his treasury to them— then gave orders for them to take as much provisions as they desired for their journey.

Furthermore, as a leader of a herd of monkeys numbering as many as lotuses in his dwelling, he— who serves the elders— appoints those who are like himself to their respective stations among the frightened, the afflicted, the young, and the old.
Thus, because he was preoccupied with rising, even though he was being urged on, he did not hasten to find fault;
for how could I have observed the falling of the shadow there, since I had not even met the Noble One? (Rc 3.47)
"First there is news of our enemy that we must know, and then there is what must be done to bring it to an end;
because of this agitation, O Noble One, my feverish preoccupation with affairs of state prevents me from maintaining my composure. (Rc 3.48)
Because they do not seek anything for themselves, because they speak figuratively, and because they conceal their true intentions, they overcome those who despise them;
by explaining the truth exactly as it is, they cause their friends to become inseparable.
Through the mutual lapse of their favor, the friendship between two wicked men turns into hostility;
yet the friendship between two virtuous men, established by the resonance of their nobility, does not perceive any fault. (Rc 3.50)
That friendship where one need not act without restraint, nor rejoice in excessive expressions of affection,
and where there is mutual suspicion and fear from afar— such friendship deserves only a distant salutation.
"Command me with confidence; what shall I do? Why does the king of monkeys, having assigned some task, now restrain me in secret as if he were regarding me with affliction? (Rāmāyaṇa 3.52)
I shall remain here for this day; tomorrow you will come, and I will not wait for your command.
Wherever my noble father does not employ me out of consideration, there I am independent, free from my mother’s restrictions.

Therefore, having gone forth, I shall act in such a way that this monkey, who was previously associated with him, may swiftly repay his noble lord for that great service which resulted in the destruction of his enemy through my efforts.
Fie on me, a mere follower with bow in hand, whose pride has been vainly nourished by my mind;
for because of my failure, the noble one, who knows the inner heart, is looking for another companion.
Fie on my arrows' sharpness, fie on their ability to bend even the highest mountains, and fie on the speed of my swift shafts,
for they do not return in an instant after slaying the enemy, even though he was not within their range of sight.
O Moon of the Earth, what else could these crescent moons do but hasten to drink once more the blood of the blood-drinkers, they whose experience of such slaughter has long been known? (Rc 3.57)
Having subdued Ātāṭakā by means of the *saṃjñapana* rite, you have indeed committed him to the protection of the social orders (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).
Let the office of destroying the night-stalkers be completed by the extermination of their remnants.
Having warded off the shower of terrible weapons that had been unleashed by the expenditure of a flood of arrows,
you alone protected the sacrifice of the great seer from the rākṣasas dwelling in the sky.
How much effort did it take for him to slay that Virādha, who was like Death itself and stood as an obstacle on the path?
And how many moments passed while he struck down the army of Svaras, the lord of Janasthāna?

How long was the delay for that razor-edged arrow upon those cruel heads of Triśiras? And how many arrows were discharged in battle for the purpose of bringing an end to Dūṣaṇa’s bodily existence? (Rāmāyaṇa-campu 3.61)
Relying on whom did the Noble One bring Mārīca—who was capable of manifold transformations—to his end?
For you yourself knew him, as he was signaled by you, and he too was the lord of the night-stalkers.

Thus, with their causes for conceptual proliferation stilled, the birds in their nests, having reached a single-minded harmony, uttered true and pleasant notes as if praising the mutual grasping of each other's genuine virtues.
Having placed the twilight in the direction of Vajrapāṇi and having cast the moon toward the western quarter,
the night departed, taking away the sleep of the birds while cradling a multitude of stars in her lap.
The poet, Jīva, Suta of the Earth, and the sage who is the ornament of the southern quarter—
for a moment protected the rear of the celestial sphere as it was being melted by the fear of the sun’s rays.
Before the eastern quarter, like an intoxicated courtesan, could show its face flushed with passion,
the lord of the twice-born (the moon) reached her lap, suspecting it to be the spray from the evening twilight.

For a moment, the moon remained with its stars cast away; even at the horizons, there was no darkness. In the direction of Indra, the twilight shone intensely, like the vermilion seal of the king of planets.
Plucking the buds of the stars aloft and manifesting an exceedingly intense passion,
the twilight ascended the tree of the sky by clinging to the branch that is the direction of Indra.
As if her passion had intensified to gather the remaining clusters of moon-blossoms, the twilight,
having stood high upon the crest of the eastern mountain, ascended the tree of the sky.
Casting off at that time the host of stars, which resembled a mass of pale-white leaves,
the tree of the sky bore clusters of blossoms in the form of the twilight’s glow, as delicate as a young woman’s lower lip.
As if driven away from the frontal globes of Airāvata by the winds presiding over Indra’s chariot,
the twilight, shimmering like the dust of a theatrical transformation, spread across the courtyard of the sky.
When passion had ascended over worldly existence, the cognitions—once bright from plunging into reality—gradually lost their luster and sank away;
the stars, too, slowly faded as the dawn spread forth.

By whom was it taught how to appear? At that moment, the youthful twilight shone forth like a painting brought to life by a brush upon a sky as vast and uneven as a mass of towering autumn clouds tossed by waves.
Just as it was first scattered across the quarter of the Lord of Gods,
the light of the young sun shone upon the surface of the sky like spreading oil upon a wave-crested mass of anointed, fragmented clouds.
Even the sky, though the sun was present, bore a redness as if it were filled with the nectar-rays of the moon brought forth by his serenity;
for the vessels of those destined for great exaltation respond to the influence of their successive circumstances.
Resembling a *tāpiñcha* flower, the deer in the western quarter covered the moon;
appearing exceedingly devoid of color, it was like a calamity befalling people who had traveled far.

Then the sky became like a city besieged by an army: with the fires of twilight ablaze, the flocks of birds crying out, the moon cast down and turned away by the naked [demons], and the clusters of stars vanished from the firmament. (Rc 3.77)
In the rivers, the darkness consisting of frost did not fear the rays of the infant sun, for it was accompanied by the cries of pairs of cranes who had celebrated a great festival of mutual glances.
Having crossed over the dark gloom of the Himalayas, that flock of birds, crying out as they flew, crossed the rivers;
drenched by the moist pollen of red lotuses and gazing at the sun reflected in the water.
Skilled in massaging every limb of the Pulinda women who were weary from the exhaustion of amorous play,
the breeze from the lake’s waves lingered within the calyxes of the lotuses and then moved on.
Having passed beyond the coldness of the riverbanks' sands, the sages bathed in the rivers that were pleasantly warm;
and the hollows of the mountain torrents were filled by the wives of the village families living in the mountain hamlets.
When the outdoor grounds were filled with light, the elephant— vigilant in the festival of unrestrained roaming—
remembered his bed in the hollow of his belly as its trunk stumbled along the ground.
Having gathered together after their yawning, and having licked one another's dewy coats for a moment with their herd-mates,
the deer of the marshlands set out toward the various quarters of the horizon, looking about as each was wont.
On the open grounds, the army of forest-dwellers drank in the sun’s fiercely blazing radiance with eyes as tremulous as stars;
and the multitude of serpents, their nostrils entering the hollows of the roots, drank it in.
At that time, the land with its wide-eyed deer and the water with its lotuses whose petals were unfurled,
as well as the water with its shimmering fish and the land with its hovering bees, bore no distinction between one another.
Having completely enjoyed the pollen from the beds of night-lotuses— whose rows of petals were widely parted by the weight of yawning and delayed by their closing— the bee departed unattached.
The supreme serpent entered the hole he had gone to, for the supreme one always dwells in the highest state;
yet, in the attainment of such greatness, no one could describe the height of his majesty, which reached even unto the heavens.
By those peaceful bees who gradually took refuge in the night-lotuses, free from attachment to the day-lotuses,
and who gathered for a long time in the abode of the day-lotuses, kindness was likewise embraced by them all equally.

At the sight of the sun, the friend of the lotuses, the beds of night-lotuses— displaying a surge of joy through their blossoming lotuses— barely endured the separation from the moon by resorting to sleep.
The moon, its redness intensified by the waters, released the pollen of the lotuses from the agitation of the lilies;
having long resided in the western quarter, it now abandoned the sky, its own western glow revealed.
Just as the sky, its clusters of stars vanished, shone with the rays of the young sun,
so too did the lake, all its night-blooming lilies asleep, shine with red lotuses on every side.
His face shone like a thousand-petaled lotus, blossoming at the light of the rising sun,
its bud-like sheath opened for the bees of Mañjuśrī’s sweet-sounding arrows to seize it of their own accord.
Some entered through the slightly opened mouths of the bees, others through the hollows of their petals;
for the swarms of honey-seeking bees among the lotuses, there was no certainty as to which entrance to choose.
The bee rolled in the dust, drank the honey, and licked again his own licked eyelashes;
though he had come as a guest, he did not grant even the slightest opening for himself within the center of the lotus.
The bird did not visit the lotus pond that was still asleep, nor did he frequent the riverbanks which lacked the glow of the new sun;
thus he returned to his beloved, though she remained deluded, for he was resentful toward the arrival of his own awakening.
That poor bird, perched near his side, offered many flattering words;
after a long time, the ruddy goose opened his eyes, which had become bloodshot from the removal of his sleep.
But the purifier [the moon], hastened by the pain of love, set out across the shore— a darkness thick with dew-drops—
while the sound of the beloved’s name, heard like the cry of a monkey, seemed to part the blooming lotus grove as he went.
The ruddy goose, longing for the embrace of his mate, went away to break off lotuses;
she too, full of eager anticipation, arrived at that very moment, surveying the forest of blue lilies.
As they performed their aimless coming and going along diverging paths in the lotus-thicket-covered lake,
falling at last toward the same direction, they somehow managed after a long time to form a pair at the halfway point.
Let the heat of the sun, which scorches like a mirage, be forgotten by the pairs of birds upon seeing the morning;
for that which is cool by nature becomes hot—indeed, nothing is fixed, as the course of things in this world depends on the condition of living beings.
Shining with a moon-like face whose smile bespoke the serenity of a mind resolved upon his duty,
Rāma went to the Pampā lake together with Lakṣmaṇa— a lake whose ripples were stirred by the morning breeze.

Having bathed well and performed his ritual duties, the descendant of Kakutstha approached the sun— which was as bright as molten gold— just as it rose, its fresh petals crimson from being torn by the agitation of the pollen stirred by the bees standing at its side.

Having performed the morning twilight devotions according to the prescribed rules for a long time, while the sun’s rays were only slightly visible upon its crest of hair, the two sat at the edge of the forest on a spot devoid of trees, where their matted locks lay motionless and undulating.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Description of the Morning Twilight Preceded by the Determination of Counsel," in the great poem *Rāmacarita* composed by the poet Abhinanda.
